guide.summary: The most heavily weighted unit (30–40%). It covers one-dimensional arrays, ArrayLists, two-dimensional arrays, standard traversal algorithms, searching (linear and binary) and sorting (selection, insertion, merge), recursion tracing, working with data sets and text files, and the ethics of data collection.

sections.heading: Arrays
sections.body: Arrays have fixed length (arr.length, no parentheses). new int[n] fills with 0, new double[n] with 0.0, new boolean[n] with false, and object arrays with null. An initializer list creates and fills an array: int[] a = {3, 8, 1}. Valid indices are 0 to length − 1; others throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. An enhanced for loop (for (int x : arr)) reads each element but assigning to x doesn't change the array. Standard algorithms: sum/average, min/max and their index, count matches, check for duplicates (nested loops), shift or rotate elements, reverse (swap from both ends), and determine if elements are in order.

sections.heading: ArrayList
sections.body: ArrayList<E> holds objects (wrapper types for primitives) and resizes dynamically. Methods: size(), add(obj), add(index, obj) (shifts later elements right), get(index), set(index, obj) (returns old value), remove(index) (shifts later elements left and returns the removed element). When removing during a forward index loop, decrement i after removal or traverse backward; otherwise the next element is skipped. Don't add or remove inside an enhanced for loop (ConcurrentModificationException).

sections.heading: 2D arrays
sections.body: A 2D array is an array of rows: int[][] g = new int[rows][cols]; g.length is the number of rows and g[0].length the number of columns; access g[r][c]. Row-major traversal: outer loop over rows, inner over columns. Column-major traversal: outer over columns, inner over rows. Enhanced for over a 2D array gives each row (an int[]). Neighbor checks must stay in bounds (0 ≤ r < rows, 0 ≤ c < cols).

sections.heading: Searching, sorting, and recursion
sections.body: Linear search checks each element: up to n comparisons. Binary search requires sorted data and halves the search range each step: about log₂ n + 1 comparisons at most. Selection sort repeatedly selects the minimum of the unsorted portion and swaps it into place; after k passes, the first k elements are the k smallest in order. Insertion sort inserts each next element into its correct place in the sorted portion on the left. Merge sort recursively splits, sorts halves, and merges; it is faster for large data. A recursive method calls itself with a smaller input and must have a base case; trace it by writing each call and combining results on the way back.

sections.heading: Data sets and files
sections.body: Programs often read data from text files (e.g., with a Scanner wrapping a File), parse lines with split, and store values in arrays or ArrayLists of objects for analysis. Data can contain errors, missing values, or bias; how data are collected and used raises privacy and fairness concerns.

keyTakeaways: Enhanced for can't modify array elements.
Removing in a forward loop skips elements unless you adjust i.
Binary search needs sorted data: ~log₂ n steps.
commonMistakes: Loop bound i <= arr.length causing out-of-bounds.
Mixing up rows and columns in 2D loops.
examTips: Q3 (ArrayList) FRQs often require removing or filtering; handle index shifts.
Q4 (2D array) FRQs: write explicit nested loops with correct bounds and stay in bounds for neighbors.
Sorting MCQs: trace the array state after each pass.
Recursion MCQs: write the call stack and evaluate bottom-up.
guide.cramSheet:
**Array:** fixed length · defaults 0/0.0/false/null · arr.length · enhanced for = read-only

**ArrayList:** size · add · add(i, x) · get · set · remove(i) shifts left · remove → i−− or go backward

**2D:** g[r][c] · g.length rows · g[0].length cols · row-major vs column-major

**Search:** linear n · binary log₂ n (sorted)

**Sort:** selection (min to front) · insertion (insert left) · merge (split, merge)

**Recursion:** base case + smaller call · trace the stack

practice.stem: Which code correctly removes every String of length less than 3 from an ArrayList<String> words?

choices.text: for (int i = words.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { if (words.get(i).length() < 3) { words.remove(i); } }
for (int i = 0; i < words.size(); i++) { if (words.get(i).length() < 3) { words.remove(i); } }
for (int i = 0; i <= words.size(); i++) { if (words.get(i).length() < 3) { words.remove(i); i--; } }

practice.explanation: Traversing backward means removals don't shift unvisited elements.

distractors.B: Modifying during an enhanced for throws an exception.
distractors.D: i <= size() goes out of bounds.

practice.prompt:
A terrain map is stored in an int[][] grid of elevations. A cell is a local peak if its value is strictly greater than every orthogonally adjacent cell (up, down, left, right) that exists. Cells on edges and corners have fewer neighbors.

Write the static method `countPeaks(int[][] grid)` that returns the number of local peaks. For example, for {{1, 5, 2}, {3, 9, 4}, {8, 2, 7}}, the peaks are 9, 8, and 7, so the method returns 3. Assume grid has at least one row and one column.

rubric.description: Nested loops visit every cell with correct bounds (grid.length and grid[0].length or grid[r].length).
Compares with the cell above and below only when those rows exist.
Compares with the cell left and right only when those columns exist.
Uses strict greater-than for all existing neighbors.
Increments a counter only when all existing neighbors are smaller.
Initializes the counter before the loops and returns it.
